oneSentence: Memorisation happens when a model encodes information specific to individual training examples or small subsets of them.
plainExplanation:
A model is trained on examples such as images, text or numbers. During training, it adjusts numerical parameters to produce outputs such as a label, score or summary.

Memorisation occurs when those parameters encode information specific to individual training examples or small subsets. This may allow exact or near-exact reproduction, or make an output depend unusually strongly on whether a particular example appeared in training.

Memorisation can coexist with learning broader patterns. It can contribute to overfitting, but a drop on new data does not by itself prove memorisation. Such a drop may instead reflect distribution shift, noise or reliance on a spurious correlation.

Memorisation is also different from long-term memory in AI systems. Long-term memory is a designed mechanism for storing and retrieving information across separate sessions. Training-data memorisation is information encoded while the model is trained.

everydayAnalogy.title: Sorting bottles by their dents
everydayAnalogy.story: Someone learns to sort reusable bottles by repeatedly seeing the same batch. Instead of noticing the bottle shapes and materials, they remember that the bottle with a torn green label goes in one crate and the bottle with a dent near the base goes in another. They are almost perfect when the familiar bottles return. With a new batch, the labels and dents are different, so the sorting quickly breaks down. The person learned details of the examples, not a rule that travels.

mapping.analogyElement: memorising particular practice photos and nearby visual quirks
mapping.aiElement: storing training examples or their distinctive details rather than learning general features

mapping.analogyElement: high score on repeated practice images
mapping.aiElement: strong performance on training data or leaked test data

mapping.analogyElement: mistakes on new images from other places and conditions
blue roof or curved shadow used as a shortcut

everydayAnalogy.limitation: A person can usually explain what they memorised and may deliberately choose to do so. A model does not usually store examples as neat labelled photos it can point to, and its behaviour comes from many numerical parameters rather than conscious study habits. Also, some reuse of training patterns is normal and useful; the problem is harmful reliance on specific seen details that does not transfer to new cases.

visual.title: Learning a general rule versus memorising training examples
visual.learningObjective: Show why two models can score well on familiar data but differ sharply on truly new data.
visual.description: A side-by-side comparison with three rows: training data, test on familiar-looking data, and test on genuinely new data. Read left to right. The left column shows a model that learns broad signs of road damage. The right column shows a model that relies on repeated image quirks from the training set.

steps.label: Same training set
steps.explanation: Both models are trained on the same labelled satellite images of roads, including damaged and undamaged sections.
steps.visualInstruction: Top row spanning both columns: small thumbnails of labelled road images feeding into two separate model boxes.

steps.label: General pattern learner
steps.explanation: The left model picks up broad features that can appear in many places, such as broken road edges, irregular dark pits and repeated crack shapes.
steps.visualInstruction: Left column middle: model box highlights several distributed features across many thumbnails, with no single image emphasised.

steps.label: Memorising learner
steps.explanation: The right model leans on specific seen details, such as one neighbourhood pattern, one lighting condition or one repeated background object.
steps.visualInstruction: Right column middle: model box highlights a few exact thumbnails and a callout around a spurious cue like roof colour or shadow shape.

steps.label: Looks fine on familiar checks
steps.explanation: If evaluation images are too similar to training data, both models can appear accurate.
steps.visualInstruction: Third row: both columns output many green ticks for a test set labelled 'very similar to training'.

steps.label: Separates on new data
steps.explanation: When the test set comes from new cities, dates or image conditions, the general-pattern model holds up better while the memorising model drops sharply.
steps.visualInstruction: Bottom row: left column shows mostly green ticks on 'new images'; right column shows a visible mix of red crosses and a lower score badge.

visual.interaction: Hovering or tapping a highlighted cue reveals whether it is a transferable feature or a training-specific shortcut.
visual.accessibilityDescription: This is a side-by-side comparison of two models trained on the same road images. The left model learns broad signs of damage that appear across many examples. The right model relies on specific details from the training images, such as a repeated background pattern or lighting cue. On a test set that looks very similar to the training set, both models seem to perform well. On a genuinely new test set with different places and conditions, the left model keeps performing relatively well, while the right model performs much worse. The diagram teaches that memorisation can hide behind good-looking results if the evaluation data are not truly independent and varied.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: A static two-column diagram shows the same comparison without animation: shared training data at the top, model behaviour in the middle, and performance on familiar versus new test data at the bottom.

workedExample.scenario: An information management officer at a regional hub checks an image classifier before using its results in a road-condition monitoring report.
workedExample.input: 1,200 labelled satellite images for training and 300 images for initial testing.
process: Many images show the same road segments on nearby dates, creating near-duplicates with similar shadows, buildings and surface markings.
A random split places related images in both sets. The model reaches 98% accuracy on the training set and 95% on the initial test set.
The officer assembles a second test set from different areas, dates and viewing angles, removing duplicate and near-duplicate images.
Accuracy falls to 68%. Errors cluster where shadows, surface colours and nearby structures differ from those in the training images.
workedExample.result: The initial score was inflated by repeated patterns and narrow visual cues. The drop on independently sampled images is consistent with memorisation and weak transfer, although further tests would be needed to establish the cause.

unWorkplaceExample.scenario: A partnerships officer at a shared services centre is finalising a handover note before close of business. She reviews a model proposed to route incoming implementing-partner queries into categories such as grant amendments, reporting and due diligence.
unWorkplaceExample.relevance: The historical inbox contains repeated templates, familiar partner names and near-duplicate follow-ups. If these appear across both training and test sets, the model may score well by recalling narrow cues rather than learning the substance of each query. It may then misroute messages from new partners or a new reporting cycle.
unWorkplaceExample.caution: Do not place correspondence containing personal data, bank details, due diligence records or procurement-sensitive material in any tool not approved for it. Use an approved environment, restrict access, remove unnecessary identifiers and duplicates, and test on later, independently sampled messages. Human review remains necessary because both disclosure and misrouting can cause harm.

whyItMatters: Memorisation matters because a system can appear reliable while actually being fragile. A polished dashboard or a high benchmark score may hide the fact that the model only works on cases that closely resemble its training data. For policy and operational use, that can lead to poor procurement choices, unfair treatment of some groups, weak risk controls and false confidence in deployment. Checking for memorisation helps you ask better questions: Was the test data truly separate? Are there duplicates or leaked clues? Does performance hold across places, languages, time periods and conditions that matter in the real task?
whereYouMayHearIt: During first reading of a model evaluation report
At a vendor demo in a procurement meeting
In an ICT governance board review of a proposed pilot
During clearance of a monitoring report that relies on model outputs

commonMisconceptions.misconception: If training accuracy is very high, the model must have learned the task well.
commonMisconceptions.correction: High training accuracy only shows the model fits the data it has already seen. It may still rely on repeated examples, accidental clues or noise. What matters is performance on well-separated, representative new data.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Memorisation and overfitting are exactly the same thing.
commonMisconceptions.correction: They are closely related but not identical. Overfitting is the broader problem of fitting too closely to training data and losing performance on new cases. Memorisation is a specific pattern within that broader problem, where the model depends heavily on seen examples or highly specific details.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Memorisation only matters for text models that repeat training sentences.
commonMisconceptions.correction: It can happen in images, tabular data, audio and other formats too. A model may memorise repeated backgrounds, camera artefacts, site names, timestamps or other shortcuts, even if it never reproduces an exact text passage.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A good benchmark score proves memorisation is not a problem.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Not necessarily. A benchmark can still be too narrow, too similar to the training data, or affected by contamination and leakage. The score is useful only if the evaluation setup matches the real use case and is properly separated from training.

simpleVsTechnical.simple: A model has memorised when it seems good mainly because it has seen very similar examples before, not because it learned a rule that works more widely.
simpleVsTechnical.technical: In technical terms, memorisation refers to a model encoding training-set-specific information strongly enough that its outputs depend on recalled examples or narrow cues rather than robust, transferable structure. This can appear as exact or near-exact reproduction, unusually high confidence on repeated patterns, sensitivity to duplicate or near-duplicate samples, or sharp performance drops under distribution shift. It is often associated with high-capacity models, limited or noisy data, and weak train-test separation. Memorisation is related to but distinct from generalisation: some retention of recurring patterns is necessary for learning, while harmful memorisation shows up when behaviour does not extend to independently sampled data from the target task. It is also linked to overfitting and can be worsened by data leakage, contamination of benchmarks, or spurious correlations. Detection often relies on holdout evaluation, deduplication, cross-validation where appropriate, out-of-distribution testing, privacy-oriented probing, and inspection of whether errors increase when superficial cues change.

keyTakeaway: A strong score may reflect recalled examples or narrow cues rather than a pattern that transfers to genuinely new cases.

quickCheck.question: Which result is the clearest warning sign of memorisation?
options: The model scores high on training data and also on a test set built from near-duplicate examples from the same source.
The model scores lower on training data than on a carefully separated test set from new regions.
The model keeps similar performance across new locations, dates and image conditions.
The model uses fewer parameters after retraining on more varied data.
quickCheck.explanation: High scores on training data and near-duplicate test data can happen even when the model has mainly learned to repeat seen patterns. The warning sign becomes stronger when the test set is not truly independent. Good evaluation uses separate, representative data and checks whether performance holds under meaningful changes.

issues.problem: The page repeatedly defines memorisation as reliance on narrow cues or failure to learn a general rule. Those are not sufficient conditions. A model can learn a spurious correlation without encoding any particular training example, and it can memorise examples while also generalising well. This blurs memorisation into overfitting, poor generalisation and shortcut learning.
issues.fix: Define memorisation as encoding information specific to individual training examples or small subsets. State that it can contribute to overfitting but can also coexist with generalisation. Do not treat distribution shift or reliance on a narrow cue as proof.

issues.problem: The distinction from long-term memory is incomplete. Saying long-term memory stores information "during use" omits its defining retrieval across separate sessions and therefore does not clearly distinguish it from training-data memorisation.
issues.fix: Memorisation is also different from long-term memory in AI systems, which stores information for retrieval across separate sessions.

issues.problem: The blue roof, curved shadow, neighbourhood pattern and lighting examples demonstrate spurious correlations or shortcut learning, not necessarily memorisation. A model could learn those dataset-wide correlations without encoding any particular photo. The analogy and diagram therefore teach the wrong mechanism.
issues.fix: Base the memorising side on exact or near-duplicate road segments recurring across training and evaluation. If roof colour and shadows remain, label them as possible shortcuts rather than as evidence of memorisation.

issues.problem: The limitation does not acknowledge the analogy's main failure: remembering a particular photo is different from learning a spurious cue shared by many photos. Its final sentence instead repeats the conflation.
issues.fix: The roof and shadow behaviour could come from a spurious correlation without the model encoding any particular photo. That would show weak generalisation, not by itself memorisation. A model also has no conscious study strategy, and encoded information is distributed across numerical parameters rather than stored as labelled photos it can point to.

issues.problem: The example does not establish that near-duplicates cross the training-test boundary. It says only that the training set contains near-duplicates and that the initial test set comes from the same collection. The drop from 95% to 68% under changes in district, date and viewing angle could result from distribution shift or spurious correlations. It does not justify the causal conclusion that memorisation partly caused the early score.
issues.fix: Either state that near-duplicates of training images appeared in the initial test set, or weaken the result to: "The score drop shows weak transfer to changed conditions, but does not by itself establish memorisation."

issues.problem: Most of this field describes the consequences and checks for poor generalisation, overfitting and data leakage. It claims these checks are for memorisation without explaining that they do not specifically establish training-example dependence.
issues.fix: Memorisation matters because encoded training examples can distort evaluation and may expose details from the training data. A high score on duplicated or contaminated test data can hide this dependence. Check whether evaluation data are truly separate and deduplicated, and whether outputs reproduce distinctive training content. Tests across places, languages, times and conditions remain important, but performance drops there show poor transfer rather than proving memorisation.

issues.problem: The phrase "a model that remembers" presents an anthropomorphic mental capacity as fact. It also equates memorisation with failure under slight real-world change, which is evidence of poor generalisation rather than memorisation specifically.
issues.fix: A model can encode or reproduce training examples while still failing on independently sampled cases.

issues.problem: Option 0 is the only defensible answer, but the quiz is weak. It identifies an evaluation setup that can conceal memorisation, not a result that specifically demonstrates it. Options 2 and 3 are obvious opposites or irrelevant, while option 1 is an unusual comparison with no plausible connection to memorisation. The answer can be selected without understanding the distinction from overfitting or poor generalisation.
issues.fix: Replace the quiz with: "Which result most specifically supports memorisation rather than poor generalisation alone?" Options: ["The model reproduces a rare erroneous phrase from one training example when given its opening words.", "Accuracy drops on images from new cameras.", "The model relies on roof colour correlated with labels.", "Training accuracy exceeds accuracy on an independent test set."]. Keep option 0 as correct.
